articles.title: Does a boggart still haunt Clegg Hall?
articles.excerpt: The old tale of the Clegg Hall boggart is a durable piece of Lancashire storytelling; the building and its ownership are historical, the murder story is not.
articles.summary: The old tale of the Clegg Hall boggart is a durable piece of Lancashire storytelling; the building and its ownership are historical, the murder story is not.
articles.body:
Clegg Hall stands where the lane named for it climbs from the Roch to Smithy Bridge: a stone, two-storey house dated by experts to about 1610 and protected as a Grade II* listed building (List Entry Number 1309615). Its architectural record — mullioned windows, a central two-storey porch and an oak‑lined interior — is clear and documented in the National Heritage List for England. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1309615))

The ghost story that gives the place its local fame is older in print than the present stone house. In the nineteenth century the folklorist John Roby published a version of the “Clegg Hall Boggart” collected from local tellers; he and others reproduced a dramatic tale in which a grasping relative murders the rightful heirs so he can take the hall. Roby’s compilation and later ballads — most notably a ballad communicated to Roby by the Rochdale writer William Nuttall — are the principal literary sources for the legend. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/25256/pg25256-images.html))

Local history writers have been sceptical. The county history and the 1889 History of the Parish of Rochdale describe the same tradition — the murdered heirs thrown into a moat or otherwise despatched — but caution that Roby’s narrative is largely imaginative and that the story survives as oral tradition rather than as a contemporaneous record. The historian’s account also records an old proverb: “As ill as Clegg Hall boggart,” showing the tale’s reach into local speech. ([your-content.s3.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com](https://your-content.s3.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/04145039/chapter-xvii-old-houses-and-old-families-butterworth-pages337-389.pdf))

What we can verify: the site, the principal dates and the ownership trail are matters of documentary record. Butterworth’s parish history traces the manor through the Belfield, Assheton and Howorth families and records the sale of the “capital messuage of Clegg called Clegg Hall” in the early 17th century. The present building’s fabric and its listing details are set out in the Historic England entry. Those facts are separate from the boggart story. ([your-content.s3.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com](https://your-content.s3.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/04145039/chapter-xvii-old-houses-and-old-families-butterworth-pages337-389.pdf))

What we cannot verify: there is no medieval court roll, inquest record or other contemporary legal document published online that proves the alleged murders happened in the thirteenth or fourteenth centuries. Folklore specialists and local investigators note that the legend exists in multiple, conflicting variants and that no surviving primary source from the medieval period corroborates the violent events told in Roby and later retellings. In short: the murders belong to tradition, not confirmed archive evidence. ([wyrdways.uk](https://wyrdways.uk/sites/clegg-hall-boggart/))

How the boggart fits regional folklore is clear. “Boggart” is a Lancashire term for a household or landscape spirit whose mischief ranges from annoying to malevolent; Clegg Hall’s boggart is one of several well‑known regional examples recorded by Victorian collectors. Those collectors shaped and sometimes embellished oral material when they wrote it down, so the written tradition mixes local memory with nineteenth‑century literary habits. ([upload.wikimedia.org](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/50/Lancashire_Folk-Lore-_Illustrative_of_the_Superstitious_Beliefs_and_Practices%2C_Local_Customs_and_Usages_of_the_People_of_the_County_Palatine_%28IA_dli.granth.84778%29.pdf))

So — does a boggart still haunt Clegg Hall? If you mean “is there a documented, contemporaneous record that a relative murdered heirs and that their restless spirits haunt the place?” the answer is no: surviving documentary history supports the house and its owners but not a proven tragedy in the medieval record. If you mean “does the tale still live in local memory?” the answer is yes: the boggart lives in printed folklore, local sayings and the imagination of visitors and readers. ([your-content.s3.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com](https://your-content.s3.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/04145039/chapter-xvii-old-houses-and-old-families-butterworth-pages337-389.pdf))

If readers want to follow the paper trail themselves, good starting points are the Historic England listing for the building and the nineteenth‑century sources that recorded the legend — John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire and the local parish history by Butterworth. Those sources separate the architectural and archival facts from the later storytelling; beyond that, the rest is local legend and lively company for a cold evening’s walk, if you like such things. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1309615))

articles.title: Rochdale Council Addresses Concerns Over Local Pub Closures
articles.excerpt: Councillor Richard Jackson has raised concerns about the future of local pubs in Littleborough after the closure of The Wheatsheaf, highlighting restrictive covenants that hinder reopening efforts.
articles.content_html:
The future of local pubs in Littleborough is under scrutiny following the recent closure of The Wheatsheaf. This closure has sparked community outcry and raised concerns about the viability of pubs in the area. Councillor Richard Jackson addressed these issues during a Rochdale council meeting on October 15, highlighting the challenges posed by restrictive covenants that prevent former pubs from being reopened as such.

Councillor Jackson noted that approximately 50 per cent of pubs are owned by breweries or large pub companies, which often include covenants in sales to deter competition. This practice has led to a significant number of closures, with many pubs being sold off for alternative uses. He cited the example of the former Royal Oak pub, which closed in 2015 and was subsequently converted into a vape shop, a change that was later halted by Trading Standards due to regulatory issues.

The council's discussion aims to address the ongoing loss of pubs in the community, with Jackson's motion seeking to reduce the impact of these covenants. He expressed concern over the cycle of tenant attrition that many pubs face, stating, "We have seen this at the former Royal Oak pub. This was sold with an anti-competition covenant."

The implications of this discussion are significant for local residents and pub enthusiasts, as the council considers measures to protect these community assets. The outcome of this motion could influence future policies regarding the sale and repurposing of pubs in Littleborough and beyond.

articles.title: Court Rules on Ownership Dispute Over Hopwood Hall
articles.excerpt: A recent court ruling has clarified the ownership of Hopwood Hall, resolving a long-standing dispute. The decision is expected to have significant implications for the local community.
articles.content_html:
A court has ruled on the ownership of Hopwood Hall, a historic site in Rochdale, following a protracted legal dispute. The ruling has clarified the ownership status of the property, which has been a matter of contention for some time.

The decision is expected to have significant implications for the local community, particularly regarding the future use and preservation of Hopwood Hall. Local stakeholders have been keenly awaiting the outcome, as it may influence future development plans for the area.

While the specifics of the ruling have not been detailed in the source material, it is anticipated that the resolution will provide a clearer path forward for the management of the hall and its grounds.

Next steps for the parties involved have yet to be confirmed, but the ruling marks a pivotal moment in the ongoing discussions surrounding Hopwood Hall's future.
